passages.t: The first three bowls, and ‘true and just’
passages.happening:
John hears a loud voice from the temple: “Go, pour out on the earth the seven bowls of God’s wrath” (verse 1).

The first angel pours out his bowl on the earth, “and loathsome, malignant sores broke out on those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image” (verse 2). The second pours his bowl into the sea, “and it turned to blood like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died” (verse 3). The third pours his bowl “into the rivers and springs of water, and they turned to blood” (verse 4).

Then John hears two voices. The angel of the waters says: “Righteous are You, O Holy One, who is and was, because You have brought these judgments. For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink, as they deserve” (verses 5-6). And the altar answers: “Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The bowls come quickly, one after another, without the long pauses that came between the sixth and seventh seals and trumpets. They follow the pattern of the trumpets, earth, sea, rivers, sun, but in full measure. The trumpets struck a third. The bowls hold nothing back.

They also follow the plagues on Egypt closely: sores, water turned to blood, and later darkness, frogs and hail. The first hearers knew that story. God had judged Pharaoh to set his people free. These pictures say that the powers which crush God's people will be judged in the same way.

Notice who is struck by the first bowl: those ‘who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image’. The bowls are aimed at the beast's kingdom and its worship.

Then the chapter stops for two voices. The angel calls God ‘Righteous’, ‘who is and was’. As in 11:17, the words ‘is to come’ are missing, because in the vision he has come. The reason given is sharp: those who poured out the blood of God's people are given blood to drink. Judgment fits the wrong.

And the altar speaks. It is the altar under which the souls of those killed for their witness cried, ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?’ (6:10). Now the answer comes from the same place: ‘true and just are Your judgments’. The Greek word for just, dikaios, includes God's faithfulness to set things right: to stand up for those who were wronged and to hold wrongdoers to account.
passages.ot:
The plagues are Egypt's. Moses “tossed it into the air, and festering boils broke out on man and beast” (Exodus 9:10). Aaron “struck the water of the Nile, and all the water was turned to blood” (Exodus 7:20). “The fish in the Nile died, and the river smelled so bad that the Egyptians could not drink its water” (Exodus 7:21).

And the praise of God's justice is Moses' song, already heard in chapter 15: “He is the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just” (Deuteronomy 32:4).
passages.hard:
Are the bowls about disasters today? Is illness, or a polluted sea, or a drought, God's judgment on the people it strikes?

Christians read the bowls in the four ways the book page sets out, as they read the seals and trumpets, and these notes do not choose. Preterists connect them with the judgments that fell on the persecuting powers of the first century, Rome or Jerusalem. Historicists have matched them with events in the church's history, one after another. Futurists read them as real judgments in a final period just before Christ returns. Idealists read them as pictures of how God's judgment on evil runs through history, and comes at last to its end.

On none of these readings do the bowls tell anyone why a particular person, town or people suffers. These notes tie no bowl to any illness, disaster, war or event of our own day. Jesus refused to read disasters that way. Of eighteen people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem?” (Luke 13:4). And nothing here makes anyone's illness or death a sign of God's judgment. When his disciples asked whose sin had caused a man's blindness, Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).

The pictures are sober. They are not to be enjoyed, and they are not given to frighten believers.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the altar where the martyrs cried ‘How long?’ is the place where God's justice is praised. Ask whether you trust God to set right what has been done to his people, without taking it into your own hands. And ask how you answer someone who calls a sickness or a disaster God's punishment on the people it struck.

passages.t: Scorching heat, and darkness on the beast's throne
passages.happening:
The fourth angel pours out his bowl on the sun, “and it was given power to scorch the people with fire” (verse 8). “And the people were scorched by intense heat, and they cursed the name of God, who had authority over these plagues; yet they did not repent and give Him glory” (verse 9).

The fifth angel pours out his bowl “on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness, and men began to gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores; yet they did not repent of their deeds” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
The fifth bowl strikes the centre: ‘the throne of the beast’. In chapter 13 the dragon gave the beast ‘his power and his throne and great authority’. Now that throne is plunged into darkness, as Egypt was. The power that seemed to see everything and rule everything cannot see at all.

Three times this chapter says that people cursed God (verses 9, 11 and 21), and twice that ‘they did not repent’ (verses 9 and 11). The word for cursing, blasphēmeō, means to slander or speak evil of. The beast blasphemed God in 13:6. Now its followers do the same. People become like what they worship.

This is a sad refrain, and it is meant to be. Pharaoh too hardened his heart after each plague. The chapter shows that pain does not by itself turn a heart to God. It can harden a person instead of breaking him. Repentance is a turning, and it is God's gift. It is not something that suffering forces out of anyone.

And notice what the refrain assumes. The chapter is grieved that they did not repent, ‘and give Him glory’. The door had been open. In chapter 11, after the witnesses were raised, ‘the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven’ (11:13). And in chapter 14 an angel carried ‘the eternal gospel’ to every nation, calling them to ‘Fear God and give Him glory’ (14:6-7). Even here, the hope was that people would turn.
passages.ot:
The darkness is Egypt's ninth plague: “So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days” (Exodus 10:22).

And the hardened heart is Pharaoh's: “When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart—he and his officials” (Exodus 9:34).
passages.asks: Ask what has hardened you, rather than softened you, when life has gone badly. Ask what you speak against when you are in pain, and what that shows about what you worship. And ask whether you believe God's kindness, more than the threat of pain, is what leads a person to turn.

passages.t: The Euphrates dried, and the place called Armageddon
passages.happening:
The sixth angel pours out his bowl “on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East” (verse 12).

John sees “three unclean spirits that looked like frogs coming out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet” (verse 13). “These are demonic spirits that perform signs and go out to all the kings of the earth, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty” (verse 14).

Then, in the middle of the vision, a voice breaks in: “Behold, I am coming like a thief.” It speaks of “the one who remains awake and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed” (verse 15).

“And they assembled the kings in the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The Euphrates was the great river on Rome's eastern frontier, and beyond it lay the Parthian empire, Rome's rival (compare 9:14). Readers in Asia feared an invasion from that direction. Some interpreters connect the scene with the rumour that Nero would come back at the head of armies from the east. There is an older story behind it too. The Greek historian Herodotus says that Cyrus the Persian took Babylon in 539 BC by turning the Euphrates aside and marching in along the riverbed. And God dried up waters for his people at the Red Sea and the Jordan. Here a river is dried, but for the kings who come against God.

Then three spirits like frogs come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet, the false trinity of chapters 12 and 13. Frogs were unclean animals under the Law, and they recall the frogs of Egypt. They come from mouths: their weapon is deceiving words, and their ‘signs’ are like the second beast's signs in chapter 13. They gather the kings ‘for battle on the great day of God the Almighty’.

Then Christ himself speaks. ‘Behold, I am coming like a thief.’ Jesus used the same picture in the Gospels, and Paul did too. The point is not secrecy but suddenness: those who are not watching will be caught unready. ‘Awake and clothed’ recalls the letter to Laodicea, told to buy white garments to cover the shame of its nakedness (3:18). In the middle of a vision about kings and armies, the word to the churches is not to calculate. It is to stay awake.

The kings are gathered at a place called, in Hebrew, Armageddon. Most take the name as Har Megiddo, ‘the mountain of Megiddo’. Megiddo was an ancient fortress guarding the pass into a great plain where armies often met. There Deborah and Barak defeated the kings of Canaan, and there King Josiah of Judah was killed by Pharaoh Neco in 609 BC, a defeat Israel long mourned. Megiddo stood in a plain and has no mountain as such, and some suggest a link with the ‘mount of assembly’ in Isaiah 14:13.

Notice that no battle is described here. The kings are only gathered. When the conflict comes, in 19:19-21 and 20:8-9, it is decided by Christ's word and by God's own act, not by armies.
passages.ot:
Megiddo was the old battlefield. “Kings came and fought; then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo” (Judges 5:19). It was also the place of grief: Pharaoh Neco “faced him and killed him at Megiddo” (2 Kings 23:29), and Zechariah spoke of mourning “as great as the wailing of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo” (Zechariah 12:11).

The drying of waters recalls the exodus: “the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land” (Exodus 14:21). And the frogs are Egypt's: “the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt” (Exodus 8:6).
passages.hard:
Is Armageddon a real battle at a real place? When will it happen?

Christians answer in more than one way, and these notes do not choose. Many futurists expect a real final gathering of armies near Megiddo before Christ returns. Preterists often connect the picture with the wars of the first century and the judgment of Rome or of Jerusalem. Historicists have matched it with various conflicts in the church's history. Idealists and many others read Armageddon as a name with a meaning: Megiddo was the classic battlefield of Israel's story, the place of both victory and tragic defeat, so the name stands for the final confrontation between God and the powers of the world, wherever and however it comes.

These notes set no date, draw no map of the last battle, and tie Armageddon, the kings of the East or the river to no nation, army, leader, war or event of our own day. Such maps have been drawn from the headlines of every generation, and every one has failed. Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Matthew 24:36). And the chapter itself turns away from speculation to readiness: in the middle of the gathering of kings, Christ says to stay awake.
passages.asks: Ask what lies are being spoken around you with the force of signs, gathering people against God. Ask what being ‘awake and clothed’ would look like for you in an ordinary week. And ask whether you are more drawn to mapping the end than to being ready for the one who is coming.

passages.happening:
The seventh angel pours out his bowl into the air, “and a loud voice came from the throne in the temple, saying, ‘It is done!’” (verse 17).

“And there were flashes of lightning, and rumblings, and peals of thunder, and a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth—so mighty was the great quake” (verse 18).

“The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations collapsed. And God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath” (verse 19). “Then every island fled, and no mountain could be found” (verse 20).

“And great hailstones weighing almost a hundred pounds each rained down on them from above. And men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The voice comes from the throne itself. “It is done!” is one Greek word, meaning it has come to pass. It recalls, with a different verb, Jesus' cry from the cross, ‘It is finished’ (John 19:30). What was won at the cross is here carried through to its end in the world.

The storm and the earthquake have closed each series of seven: the seals at 8:5, the trumpets at 11:19. Here they come at their greatest. Earthquakes were real terrors in the province of Asia. Tacitus records one in AD 17 that destroyed twelve cities in a night, and Laodicea was levelled about AD 60. The first hearers knew what it was to see a city fall.

‘The great city’ splits in three, and ‘God remembered Babylon the great’. To be remembered by God can be the best of words, as when he remembered Noah (Genesis 8:1), or the most searching. The cup Babylon made the nations drink is now given to her (14:8, 10). Chapters 17 and 18 will slow down and show her fall at length.

The hailstones are said to weigh a talent each, a large ancient weight; the BSB gives it as almost a hundred pounds. Hail was a weapon of God in Israel's story, in Egypt and in Joshua's battle at Beth-horon.

And the chapter ends where its refrain has led. People ‘cursed God’. The last bowl brings the series to the edge of the end, and still the hearts that worshipped the beast do not turn.
passages.ot:
The hail is Egypt's: “The hail was so severe that nothing like it had ever been seen in all the land of Egypt from the time it became a nation” (Exodus 9:24). And it fell on Israel's enemies in Joshua's day: “the LORD cast down on them large hailstones from the sky” (Joshua 10:11).

The cup of God's wrath was the prophets' picture of judgment on proud powers, and Revelation has already used it for Babylon (14:8-10), drawing on Jeremiah: “Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk” (Jeremiah 51:7).
passages.hard:
A word for anyone frightened by this chapter.

These pictures were given to suffering churches, to tell them that the powers crushing them would not escape God's justice. They are not aimed at frightened believers, and they are not given so that anyone will live in dread. The bowls fall on the beast's kingdom, on those who bear its mark and worship its image (verse 2). In the middle of them, Christ speaks to his own: stay awake. And the people who refuse to turn in this chapter are those who go on cursing God. A person who is afraid of being far from God, and wants to come near, is not in that place.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the last word from the throne in this chapter echoes the last word from the cross. Ask what you are building that would fall if the great city fell. And ask whether this chapter leaves you more afraid, or more ready, and what Jesus' word in verse 15 asks of you.
